Once a stimulus set exists, something has to present it. `lexsync` generates that
experiment from a declarative description of the trial, sparing the hand-coding
that usually follows selection. A trial is a list of events, each event says what
appears and for how long and whether a hardware trigger rides on its onset, and
each presentation target is an interpreter of that same list. The arrangement is
what lets one engine serve several paradigms and three targets: a new paradigm is
a new event list, not new backend code.

This vignette covers the event model, the paradigm registry, the three targets
and how they differ, the trigger timing that motivates the design, and how to add
a paradigm. It runs on the bundled English example lexicon and writes everything
to a temporary directory.

```{r setup}
library(lexsync)
schema <- yaml::read_yaml(
  system.file("extdata", "schema.yaml", package = "lexsync")
)
lex <- load_lexicon(
  system.file("extdata", "en_example.csv", package = "lexsync"),
  schema, language = "english"
)
pool <- build_pool(lex, list(length = c(3, 7), frequency = c(3.8, 7.0)))

design <- list(
  name = "vignette_experiment", language = "english", n_per_condition = 12,
  paradigm = "factorial",
  conditions = list(
    list(name = "high", define_by = list(frequency = c(5.2, 7.0))),
    list(name = "low",  define_by = list(frequency = c(3.8, 4.4)))
  ),
  match_on = list("length", "n_density", "old20"),
  counterbalance = list(lists = 1)
)
stim <- match_stimuli(pool, design, schema)
stim <- counterbalance(stim, design, schema)
head(stim[, c("trial", "list", "set", "condition", "word")], 3)
```

## The trial-event model

A design's trial is a list of events. Each event is a plain list whose `type`
selects the behaviour and whose remaining fields parameterise it. The factorial
paradigm's default sequence is a fixation cross, the word, a response window and
a blank.

```{r events}
events <- resolve_events(design)
str(events)
```

`resolve_events()` is the accessor the backends use, and it embodies the
precedence rule: a design's own `events` list wins, and only if there is none does
the design inherit its paradigm's default sequence. The eight event types are
`fixation`, `text`, `mask`, `blank`, `region_by_region`, `response`, `question`
and `feedback`. The first four draw something (or nothing, for `blank`) for the
event's duration. `response` and `question` collect a keypress. `region_by_region`
presents a segmented sentence one region at a time, advancing on a key.
`feedback` scores the keypress just collected and reports it, and is described
under practice blocks below.

Durations are given in milliseconds, as `duration_ms`. That is the unit a
methods section reports and the unit all three targets present, so a design asks
for the same interval wherever it runs. How closely each target delivers it
differs, as described below. A visual stimulus can still only appear on a
refresh, so the PsychoPy script measures the display's refresh rate when it starts
and converts each duration into the nearest whole number of flips: 50 ms is three
flips at 60 Hz and seven at 144 Hz. The trigger stays bound to the flip.

The other two targets time their events differently. The generated OpenSesame
experiment builds every canvas of a trial before the trial starts and times each
event from the onset its display returns. It ends the event half a frame before its
duration is up, so that the next display lands on the refresh that ends it. On a
simulated display at 60, 120 and 144 Hz, the prime and the mask of the `priming`
paradigm then last the flips the PsychoPy script gives them. Its 83 ms
stimulus-onset asynchrony stays 83.3 ms at all three rates. A duration within a
millisecond or so of halfway between two whole numbers of flips can still come out
a flip longer or shorter than in PsychoPy. In the browser, timing varies with
the machine and the browser, and primes of 33 to 50 ms are not reliably realised
online. Whatever the target, verify the timing a study depends on with a photodiode,
as described under checking the timing below.

A duration may also be given as `duration_frames`, as several registered
paradigms give theirs, and an event that gives both uses `duration_ms`. A frame
count is converted to milliseconds when the design loads, at
`presentation.assumed_refresh_hz` in the schema (60 by default), so it means the
rate the count was written for, whatever rate the experiment then runs at. The
`timeout_ms` of a response window is always in milliseconds, because a response
deadline is not tied to the refresh.

A text event's `case`, `upper` or `lower`, sets the letter case its text is shown
in. The runners apply it as they show the text, with `str.upper()` and
`str.lower()` in PsychoPy and OpenSesame and `toUpperCase()` and `toLowerCase()` in
jsPsych, so the loop tables and the data files keep each item as it was written.
lexsync never changes the case itself, because `toupper()` leaves the German sharp
s as it is where Python and JavaScript give "SS", and the two engines must write the
same files. A mask's `length_of` names fields of the trials, and its one-character
content is repeated as many times as the longest of their values has characters,
counted when the experiments are written:

```yaml
- type: mask
  content: '#'
  length_of: [prime, target]
  duration_ms: 500
```

The count is in characters, not bytes, over every trial of every list, so each
target and each list shows the same mask.

### When a response is collected

A response event after a text event collects its key from that stimulus's onset.
The stimulus stays on screen for its duration at most and a blank follows it. The
window closes once the stimulus's duration and the response's `timeout_ms` have
both passed, so the factorial design here collects for 2,800 ms from the word's
onset. A key pressed while the word is still visible counts, the first key ends the
trial, and every target times the reaction from the word's onset.

A design that asks the participant to wait, as a delayed-response EEG design does,
keeps a window that opens once the stimulus has gone:

```yaml
- type: response
  keys: [f, j]
  timeout_ms: 2000
  from: offset
```

A stimulus that should stay on screen for the whole window, as the
`masked_priming` target does, takes the window's length as its duration, and its
response a `timeout_ms` of 0.

A response after any other event gets the same window by default, so one that
follows a blank keeps the window it had, timed from the window's own onset.
`from: onset` after such an event is refused, since a window from the onset opens
with a text event and none comes right before it. The datasheet records each
response window as `presentation$response_windows`, and its Methods text says when
responses were collected.

### Instructions and the response mapping

Every generated experiment shows instructions and waits for the space bar before
its first trial. The participant reads them at their own pace, and the
experimenter can start the run when the participant is ready. A design gives its
own text under `instructions`, which may hold line breaks:

```yaml
instructions: |
  You will see a string of letters.
  Press F if it is a real English word and J if it is not.
```

The text is carried as data: JSON in the PsychoPy script and the jsPsych page, and
an escaped literal in the OpenSesame script, so nothing in it can become code. A
control character other than the line break is refused. Without the key, lexsync
writes English instructions for the tasks it knows. A lexical decision names the
keys for a word and a pseudoword. A categorisation says that its first key means
yes and its second no, and a comprehension question says the same of its keys. Any
other design, the factorial one here among them, is told only which keys to press,
and its run log asks for instructions that say what each key means. The run log
also notes a design in another language that gives no text of its own. The
targets' own short messages, such as the prompt to press the space bar, are in
English.

A lexical decision maps word to its response event's first key and pseudoword to
its second. The paradigm's events therefore map word to the left arrow key, and
`design_en_lexdec_blocks.yaml`, whose events use f and j, maps word to f, as its
practice table does. A design may give its own mapping, with keys its response
event allows, and may rotate it across lists:

```yaml
response_mapping: {word: j, pseudoword: f}
rotate_mapping_by_list: true
```

Rotated, list *k* moves each key *k* - 1 places along the response event's keys,
which with two keys swaps them in every even-numbered list, and each version's
instructions name its own keys. lexsync refuses a mapping that names a key the
response event does not allow. It also refuses one that gives no key for a
condition whose trials name no answer, and one that names a condition no trial has.

`export_experiments()` gives each trial its correct key in `answer` as it assigns
the trigger codes, so every trial of a lexical decision can be scored. A practice
or filler table keeps its own answers, and the run log notes any that the mapping
contradicts, as a rotated mapping does in its even-numbered lists. The stimuli file
does not change. jsPsych records a key by the browser's name for it, so the jsPsych
page names each answer that way, `arrowleft` for `left`, and in every target a
correct response equals its trial's answer. The datasheet records the mapping as
`presentation$response_mapping`, and its Methods text says which key the
participants pressed for which condition.

### Content and field references

An event's `content` is either a literal or a reference to a column of the trial
table. A reference is a single field name in braces, and it is what makes an
event list a template: one list serves every trial in the design.

```{r content}
lapply(events[1:2], function(ev) ev$content)
```

The fixation event's content is the literal `+`, which every trial shows.
The text event's content is `{word}`, so each trial shows its own row's `word`
column. `required_fields()` resolves the references into the columns a design's
items must actually carry, which is how a design's item table is validated before
anything is generated.

```{r required-fields}
required_fields(design)
required_fields(list(paradigm = "priming"))
required_fields(list(paradigm = "self_paced_reading"))
```

Presented strings are always carried as data. Each target writes a trial table and
reads the strings from it at run time, and they are never interpolated into generated
code. That is why an apostrophe in a stimulus cannot break a generated script, and
it is enforced on the way in: `load_items()` rejects control characters and
over-long values in the fields a paradigm presents.

### Triggers on an event

An event may carry a `trigger`. Three forms are accepted, and the choice of form
is the choice of what the EEG marker will mean.

```{r triggers-in-events}
priming_events <- PARADIGMS$priming$events
or_dash <- function(x) if (is.null(x)) "-" else as.character(x)
data.frame(
  type = vapply(priming_events, function(e) e$type, character(1)),
  content = vapply(
    priming_events, function(e) or_dash(e$content), character(1)
  ),
  trigger = vapply(priming_events, function(e) or_dash(e$trigger), character(1))
)
```

The literal integer 20 on the prime marks every prime with the same code, since
what is being timestamped is the prime's appearance, whichever prime it is. The
token `"condition"` on the target resolves per trial to that trial's condition
code, which is the marker an ERP analysis will epoch on. The token `"item"`
resolves to a per-item code. Events with no trigger send nothing.

A literal code must be a whole number from 1 to 255, the values one byte on the
port can carry. Anything else, a misspelt token such as `"conditon"` included, is
refused when the experiment is generated, with a message naming the event. A literal
of 254 or 255, which the PsychoPy and OpenSesame experiments send when the session
starts and ends, is reported then. One equal to a condition code the design sends is
reported too, as is one within the range of the item codes it sends.

The tokens are resolved by `assign_triggers()`, which computes the codes and adds
them as columns.

```{r assign-triggers}
trig <- assign_triggers(stim)
unique(trig[, c("condition", "condition_trigger")])
range(trig$item_trigger)
```

Condition codes start at 101 and count up in order of first appearance, unless
`assign_triggers()` is given the order through its `conditions` argument. The
order of first appearance in a shuffled trial list depends on the seed, so an
analysis that decodes the codes should not rely on it. `export_experiments()`
therefore passes the order of the design's `conditions` entries, and the
pipeline does the same, adding any other condition in the order the item source
lists it, such as the words before the pseudowords of a generated lexical
decision. The first condition the design lists is always 101, whatever the seed.

```{r assign-triggers-order}
unique(assign_triggers(stim, conditions = c("high", "low"))[
  , c("condition", "condition_trigger")])
```

Item codes run from 40 upwards in code-point order of the set labels, and once a
design has ten sets or more that order is not the numeric one. With sets 1 to 20,
set 10 takes 41 and set 2 takes 51. Decode an item code through the loop table,
which pairs each trial's set with its code, and never from the label.

```{r item-codes}
twenty <- assign_triggers(data.frame(condition = "a", set = 1:20))
stats::setNames(twenty$item_trigger, twenty$set)
```

Item codes stay below 240, since a code is one byte and 254 and 255 mark the
session. A design may send item codes together with condition codes, or with a code
of its own from 40 to 239. Its item codes are then drawn from the codes those leave
free, skipping 101 upwards and the design's own codes. Otherwise, sets 65 and 66 of
a 70-set design would take 101 and 102, and an analysis that cuts its epochs at the
condition codes would also catch two items. Such a design is refused when it has
more item sets than free codes, unless the schema sets
`triggers.allow_code_overlap: true`, which lets the item codes wrap and repeat
within the free codes. Any other design takes its item codes from 40 upwards, in
code-point order of the set labels. They wrap at 200 values, so a design with more
than 200 item sets reuses item codes.


### Timing that varies from trial to trial

A duration need not be the same on every trial. An event may instead declare a
`duration:` block, in one of two forms:

```yaml
- type: text
  content: '{prime}'
  duration: {from_column: prime_ms}          # read per trial from the items
- type: blank
  duration: {jitter: [400, 800], as: iti_ms} # drawn per trial, in milliseconds
```

The two exist for different reasons. A duration read from a column is a
manipulated variable. Here it is the prime's duration, which with the mask that
follows sets the stimulus-onset asynchrony, the lever that separates automatic
from strategic processing. It belongs in the item table and in the analysis. A
jittered duration is not manipulated at all. It decorrelates the design matrix,
as EEG and fMRI designs routinely require.

Neither draws a random number. A jittered value is a uniform integer keyed on the
seed, the column name, the list, the set and the condition, so both engines
realise the same milliseconds and a rerun reproduces them. Naming the column in
the key is what makes two jittered events draw independently, since without it
they would share a single value.

Either form writes the realised milliseconds into the stimuli table and the loop
table, because timing that varies is a variable the analysis needs, not
presentation detail. `config/design_en_priming_jitter.yaml` is a worked
example carrying both. Its prime lasts `prime_ms` and a 33 ms mask follows, so its
stimulus-onset asynchrony is `prime_ms` plus 33 ms.

Every value read from a column must be a finite number of milliseconds, not
negative. A blank or negative cell is refused, naming the column and the trial's set
and condition. Left alone, it would give an experiment that stops at the blank or
shows the stimulus for no time at all. Fractional milliseconds, such as the
33.333333 that an item table built on 60 Hz frames carries, are rounded once with
the rounder both engines share and written back. The stimuli, the loop tables and
all three targets then present the same whole milliseconds, and the run log counts
the values rounded. A fixed `duration_ms` or `duration_frames` is checked the same
way, and the lower bound of a jitter must not be negative.

## The paradigm registry

A paradigm bundles a default event sequence with the fields it needs and the
recipe for counterbalancing it. `PARADIGMS` is the registry, and it is exported,
so it can be read to see exactly what a design will inherit.

```{r registry}
names(PARADIGMS)
data.frame(
  paradigm = names(PARADIGMS),
  fields = vapply(
    PARADIGMS,
    function(p) paste(p$stimulus_fields, collapse = ", "),
    character(1)
  ),
  counterbalance = vapply(
    PARADIGMS, function(p) p$counterbalance, character(1)
  ),
  n_events = vapply(PARADIGMS, function(p) length(p$events), integer(1)),
  row.names = NULL
)
```

`factorial` shows a matched word per trial. `lexical_decision` is the same shape
but presents a `target`, which is a real word or a generated pseudoword.
`priming` is backward pattern-masked: a 50 ms prime and a 33 ms `#####` mask come
before the target, so the stimulus-onset asynchrony is 83 ms at 60 Hz. There is no
forward mask, and prime and target keep the item table's letter case.
`masked_priming` has the arrangement of Forster and Davis (1984): a forward mask of
hash marks, a brief prime in lower case and the target in upper case. The mask has
as many marks as the longest prime or target has characters. By default, lexsync
shows it for 500 ms, the prime for three frames (50 ms at 60 Hz) and the target
until the response or for 2,000 ms. Without the forward mask, a prime of
50 ms is usually visible. The change of case keeps a related prime and its target
from sharing their visual form, so that priming does not arise from the overlap of
the two displays. `self_paced_reading` replaces the word event with a
region-by-region sentence and adds a comprehension question. `categorisation` shows
a category cue and then the word to judge against it.

`design_en_rastle_repro.yaml` uses `masked_priming` for the Rastle, Davis and New
(2004) reproduction, a lexical decision whose nonword targets are fillers with the
right arrow key as their answer, while its response mapping puts both priming
conditions on the left. `design_en_andrews_repro.yaml` runs the Andrews (1989)
reproduction as a lexical decision the same way, with one pseudoword per selected
word. Both designs' comments say how the fillers were made and what still differs
from the original studies.

That last one is worth a paragraph, because what separates it from lexical
decision is not the shape of the trial but where the question lives. The cue is
a trial event, shown afresh each time, since the category varies from trial to
trial, and crossing one word with two cues is how a categorisation study
separates a property of the word from the demands of the task. A robin is a bird
quickly and an animal slowly, and only the question changed. Its `answer` field
holds the key that is correct on the trial, so scoring is a string comparison
against the recorded response with nothing to look up in whatever language the
analysis is written in. Because the paradigm requires the field, the PsychoPy and
OpenSesame targets can score each response against it, and the jsPsych data rows
carry it beside the response. A categorisation also needs 'no' trials, or pressing
the yes key on every trial scores perfectly. In `design_en_categorisation.yaml`, 16
foils, nouns that do not belong to the category they appear under, are fillers with
the answer j.

The `counterbalance` entry is the part that is easy to overlook and important to
get right. The factorial recipe shows every matched item and splits the matched
sets across lists. The Latin-square recipe exists because `priming`,
`masked_priming`, `self_paced_reading` and `categorisation` have a property the
word paradigms do
not: the same target appears in more than one condition. Showing a participant
both the related and the unrelated version of one target would let them see the
manipulation, and showing the same word under both category cues would turn the
second presentation into a repetition-priming trial. The Latin square gives each
item exactly one condition per list and rotates it across lists, so no target
repeats within a list.

```{r counterbalance-recipes}
table(list = stim$list, condition = stim$condition)
```

The paradigm decides the recipe whether or not a design lists its own events. A
design's events have no say in it, so a priming design that reads its prime's
duration from the items keeps its Latin square. `counterbalance.recipe` names a
recipe outright, `factorial` or `latin_square_target`, for a design that needs the
other one. The factorial recipe refuses more lists than item sets, since the surplus
lists would be empty.

A Latin-square rotation is complete only when the lists and the item sets are
multiples of the number of conditions. One list confounds item and condition, since
every participant sees each item in the same condition. Two lists for three
conditions show each item in only two of them, and nine items in two conditions
leave each list with five trials in one condition and four in the other. The run
log and the datasheet report such a rotation, and the Methods text calls it
incomplete. `counterbalance.incomplete: error` refuses it instead, set in the
design or, for every design, in the schema. The datasheet's `counterbalancing`
record gives the recipe that ran, the lists the stimuli table holds, whether the
rotation is complete and the trials each list gives each condition.

### Trial orders and runs of one condition

One seed gives each list one order, and every participant given that list meets
it, so each item sits at the same serial position for all of them. The order also
has runs of one condition as long as a uniform shuffle gives. Over seeds 1 to 1000
of a lexical decision with 60 words and 60 pseudowords, the longest run had a
median of 7 and a maximum of 21. A run of seven is seven trials in a row with the
same correct key. Two keys change this, and both are off by default.

```yaml
counterbalance:
  lists: 2
  max_run: 2
  orders: 3
```

`max_run: k` caps every run of one condition at k trials, or of one value of the
column `run_on` names, where a missing value counts as a value of its own. The
repair keeps as much of the seeded order as the limit allows. Each step takes the
earliest remaining trial in the seeded order that neither extends the current run
beyond k nor leaves the rest of the list unable to keep the limit. This is the kind
of sequence constraint that pseudorandomisation programs such as Mix impose (van
Casteren & Davis, 2006). The look-ahead matters. Without it, the repair ran out of
trials near the end of 931 of 1,000 seeded orders of a list of 40 words and 80
pseudowords at k = 2, a limit that some order of that list keeps. With it, only a
limit that no order can meet is refused, and the message gives the counts that rule
it out, such as 80 pseudoword trials against 40 others at k = 1. With fillers, the
limit applies to the order they are interleaved in, and the practice trials keep it
on their own.

`orders: m` writes m orders of each list into the loop tables, as `order_1` to
`order_m`, each trial's position in each order. Order 1 is the seeded order, and
orders 2 to m are ranked by the same digest with the order's number in the key,
each repaired under `max_run`. The experiments choose an order by participant
number. Participant *p* runs version `((p - 1) mod V) + 1` in order
`(((p - 1) div V) mod m) + 1`. The participants given one version therefore meet
its orders in turn, and a run without a participant number runs order 1.
OpenSesame, whose loop presents its table in file order, gets one experiment per
version and order. The orders travel inside the loop tables, which both engines
write byte for byte, so the browser page needs no hashing of its own. The
datasheet's `counterbalancing` record gives the limit, the longest run realised in
each version and the number of orders, and the Methods text states them.

```{r trial-orders}
limited <- utils::modifyList(design, list(counterbalance = list(lists = 1, max_run = 2,
                                                                 orders = 2)))
ordered <- counterbalance(stim, limited, schema)
head(ordered[order(ordered$order_2), c("trial", "order_1", "order_2", "condition", "word")])
```

### Balanced list assignment

The factorial deal sends set 1 to list 1, set 2 to list 2 and so on. That is
reproducible, but it balances nothing: every *n*th set lands in the same list, so
a dimension that happens to vary smoothly across sets is dealt out unevenly, and
where each list goes to a different group of participants, the unevenness is
confounded with the group.

`counterbalance.optimise` searches instead for an assignment whose lists have
near-equal totals on the dimensions you name, by exchanging pairs of item sets
between lists. List sizes are preserved, since a swap trades one set for another.

```yaml
counterbalance:
  lists: 4
  optimise: true
  balance_on: [length, n_density, old20, frequency]
```

`balance_on` defaults to `match_on`, and the example widens it deliberately.
Frequency is the manipulated variable and so is not matched on, but it is
manipulated *within* a list, since every list holds both conditions. Equating the
lists on its total therefore costs the manipulation nothing and removes a
difference between the participant groups who receive different lists. Naming only
the matched dimensions leaves frequency dealt arbitrarily, and measurably so: on
the shipped design the optimiser then improves the three named dimensions and
makes frequency worse than the arbitrary deal had it. Balance what you want
equated across lists, which is usually everything.

This is a steepest descent to a local optimum, not a global search. What it
guarantees is that no single exchange would improve matters further, unless
`counterbalance.max_passes`, 500 passes by default, stops the search first, in
which case the datasheet and the run log say so and a higher bound may balance the
lists further. The datasheet records the imbalance before and after, so the
improvement is checkable. The objective is all-integer and ties are broken by the
seeded keyed hash, which
keeps the two engines on the same assignment and stops list 1 being favoured for
being numbered first.

It is off by default, and stays off. Switching it on changes which items a
participant sees, so it has to be a deliberate design decision. A package
upgrade must never make that change for a study that is already running. It is
refused on a Latin-square design, where every item already appears in every list
and the lists are balanced on the items by construction. `balance_lists()` runs
the search alone if you want the assignment without applying it, and
`design_en_balanced_lists.yaml` is the worked example.

Each dimension is counted in a unit of its own before the totals are compared. By
default the unit is the dimension's mean, which suits ratio scales only, since a
dimension then weighs in proportion to its SD over its mean and so depends on where
its scale starts. Zipf frequency starts near 3, and on the shipped design it counts
for least of the four dimensions. Written as Zipf - 3, it would move 22 of the 40
item sets to another list. `counterbalance.scale: mad` counts each dimension's
deviations from its mean in units of its mean absolute deviation. The values are
rounded to hundredths first, so adding a constant that is a whole number of
hundredths leaves the lists as they were. The default stays `mean` so that a study
already running keeps its lists, and under `mad` the datasheet and the Methods
paragraph name the scale.

## Practice, fillers and feedback

Everything above treats one frame as both the materials record and the thing that
runs. That holds only while the two are the same trials, and they usually are not.
Practice exists to settle the participant into the task and is discarded before
analysis. Fillers exist to dilute the manipulation so the participant cannot guess
it, and are likewise not analysed. Both have to reach the generated experiment,
and neither belongs in the stimuli file, the descriptives or the realised control.

The pipeline therefore splits. The stimuli CSV and the reports are written from
the main rows. The PsychoPy, OpenSesame and jsPsych experiments are generated from
every presented trial. A `block` column marks which is which, and it appears only
when a design declares the blocks, so a design without them keeps exactly the
columns it had.

```yaml
practice:
  path: items/practice_en_lexdec.csv
fillers:
  path: items/fillers_en_lexdec.csv
```

Where each block goes is a methodological choice. Practice comes first, as its
own run, ordered within itself by the seeded keyed hash, so every participant
given a list and trial order meets the practice items in one fixed order. Fillers are interleaved
with the main trials, because a
block of fillers at the end is not a filler at all: it is a second block the
participant can tell apart. They are merged in before the order is drawn, so one
deterministic shuffle mixes them through, which does renumber the main trials.
That is correct, since adding fillers changes the sequence and the stimuli file
records where each item actually appeared. Both blocks appear in every list and
neither is counterbalanced, because they carry no manipulation to rotate and
every participant should get the same practice. In a resampled design, the copy
of a list in each replicate is a presentation version of its own, and it gets both
blocks too. The PsychoPy and jsPsych runners pause where the practice trials end
and nowhere else, since a pause around a filler would set it apart.

Each block's item table is read with the same validation as any other, and given a
`set` range that cannot collide with the main items, which a naive read would not
manage since practice item 1 and main item 1 would both be set 1. The counts and
the tables' checksums go into the datasheet, because what the participant saw is
part of the materials even when it is not part of the analysis.

A `feedback` event scores the trial and shows the result. It reads the field named
by `answer`, compares it as a string with the key the participant pressed, and
displays `correct`, `incorrect` or `no_response` for `duration_ms`.

```yaml
- type: feedback
  answer: answer
  correct: 'Correct'
  incorrect: 'Incorrect'
  no_response: 'Too slow'
  duration_ms: 600
  blocks: [practice]
```

`blocks:` restricts an event to the named blocks, and this is its main use:
feedback during practice confirms the mapping the instructions state, and would
contaminate reaction times in the task itself. The restriction has to be expressed
on the event because the event list is global to the design. Since a feedback event
scores a keypress, something before it must have collected one. A design whose
feedback event has no preceding `response` or `question` is refused when the
experiment is generated. Left to run time, that one design error would surface as
three different failures, one per target. `design_en_lexdec_blocks.yaml` puts all of
this together.

## The three presentation targets

The same rendered event list feeds all three exporters, so the procedure is the
same in each. What differs is what the platform can do.

```{r export}
out <- file.path(tempdir(), "lexsync_experiment")
dir.create(out, showWarnings = FALSE)
files <- export_experiments(stim, design, schema, out)
basename(unlist(files[c("psychopy", "opensesame", "jspsych")]))
```

`export_experiments()` calls `assign_triggers()` first, then each exporter, and
returns the three experiment scripts, with every file it wrote listed as `files`.
The directory holds more than the scripts, and the difference is the interesting
part.

```{r export-dir}
list.files(out)
```

PsychoPy and OpenSesame read their trials at run time from tables written beside
them, which is why CSVs appear alongside the three scripts. PsychoPy has one and
OpenSesame two, since its text travels apart from its loop table for the reason
given below. The jsPsych target has no second file, because it embeds its trials
in the HTML. That single file is enough to reproduce the procedure in a browser.

Two schema settings shape the display. `presentation$text_height_px`, a whole
number from 8 to 400 and 48 by default, is the height of the stimulus text in
pixels in all three targets. In OpenSesame, the setting is the experiment's
`font_size`, which every screen uses, the instructions included.
`presentation$fullscreen`, true by default, runs the PsychoPy script full screen, as
PsychoPy's advice on reducing dropped frames recommends. With false, the script
opens a 1280 x 1024 window. OpenSesame takes
full screen from the mode it is launched in.

PsychoPy (Peirce et al., 2019) is the reference target. The generated script
carries the event list as embedded JSON and interprets it, and it writes onset
triggers to the parallel port, or to a serial device, locked to the flip. It is the
target to use for EEG.

The script reads keys from PsychoPy's `keyboard` module. A response window opens on
a flip, where the keyboard's clock is reset and its queue cleared, so a reaction
time runs from that flip and a key pressed before it does not count. Before the
first trial, the script shows the version's instructions and waits for the space
bar. Escape there ends the run before a data file is opened. Each run
writes a data file under `data/` beside the script, named
`<base>_p<participant>_v<version>_<date>-<time>.csv`, without the `_p` part when no
participant number is given. It holds one row per trial, written as the trial ends,
so a run stopped with escape leaves a valid file of the trials it completed. A row
gives the participant, the version, the replicate and the list, then the trial's
own fields and trigger codes, then what the trial recorded. `response`, `rt_ms` and
`timed_out` hold the key, its reaction time in milliseconds and whether the window
closed without one. The reaction time runs from the onset of the stimulus the key
answers, or from the opening of a window kept with `from: offset`. `correct` says
whether the key was the trial's `answer`. It is 0 after a timeout and empty when the
trial names no answer. In a design without a response event, the question's key is
the one scored. `region_rts_ms` holds each self-paced reading region's time, joined
by `|`, and `question_response` and `question_rt_ms` the question's key and
reaction time. Near its end, the row gives the measured `refresh_hz` and
`trigger_mode`, which is `hardware` when the codes went to the device and `mock` when
they were printed. It ends with `event_flips` and `event_onsets_ms`: the flips each
event took and the time of its first flip from the trial's first, joined by `|` in
event order. A stimulus that collects its response counts the blank after it as
well, up to the key or the close of the window. The realised durations can be
checked against the declared ones there.

OpenSesame (Mathôt et al., 2012) is generated as a complete plain-text `.osexp`,
block by block, with each event becoming an inline script. Each script builds its
canvases before the trial runs, in its prepare phase, and its event is timed from the
onset its display returns. It gets its trigger by a different route, discussed
below. Its setup opens the device `triggers$backend` names, the parallel port or the
serial port `triggers$serial_port`, and follows `triggers$mode` when it cannot, as
described under trigger timing below. By default, it prints the codes and carries
on, so the experiment still runs on a machine without the hardware, and an inline
script after the setup, `lexsync_trigger_notice`, says so before any other screen.
OpenSesame takes full screen or a window from the mode it is
launched in, whatever the generated file's `fullscreen` line says.

OpenSesame also evaluates what its loop table holds. In both versions, a cell
holding `[=...]` runs as Python, and so does one holding a single `{` in
OpenSesame 4.x, where it is read as an f-string, or starting with `=` in 3.3.
Both versions retype a word such as `nan` or `007`, and 4.x shows `True` as 1. In
4.x, `infinity` and `nan`, both in the English lexicon, stop the session. An item
table passed between laboratories could otherwise run code on the machine that
presents it.

The loop table, `vignette_experiment_english_opensesame.csv` here, therefore
holds numbers only: `lexsync_row`, the trial's position in loop order, with
`lexsync_trial`, `lexsync_list`, `lexsync_set`, the trigger codes,
`critical_region` and any per-trial duration. The prefix matters because
OpenSesame 4 makes every loop column a global of the inline scripts, where `list`
and `set` would shadow Python's built-in functions of those names. The presented
text, `condition`, `block` and `answer` are in
`vignette_experiment_english_opensesame_text.csv`, which the setup script reads
with Python's `csv` module, and each script looks up its trial's row by
`lexsync_row`. Copy both files with the experiment. A value in a numeric column
that is not a plain number is refused when the experiment is generated. The
feedback script reads the response without evaluation, so a timeout shows its
`no_response` text in both versions. These rules were checked against the
sources of OpenSesame 3.3.14 and 4.1.20.

```{r opensesame-tables}
opensesame_csv <- file.path(out, "vignette_experiment_english_opensesame.csv")
names(read.csv(opensesame_csv))
names(read.csv(sub("\\.csv$", "_text.csv", opensesame_csv)))
```

OpenSesame writes nothing to its log file without a logger item, so every trial
ends with one, `lexsync_logger`, which writes every variable. The word and its
response window are one inline script. It shows the word, sends the trigger, then
flushes the keyboard and polls it while the word is shown and over a blank screen
after it. It sets `response`, `response_time` (from the word's onset), `timed_out`
and `correct`, the last scored against the trial's `answer` by the script itself.
OpenSesame's own `correct_response` is not used, since its variable syntax differs
between 3.3 and 4.x. A response kept after the stimulus with `from: offset` is a
`keyboard_response` after a blank screen, followed by a script that sets `timed_out`
and `correct`. A `keyboard_response` runs none of lexsync's code, so the script that
shows the blank first holds out a code still held. After a stimulus shorter than the
hold, the window therefore opens when the hold is up, and `response_time`, which
OpenSesame times from the item's start, runs from there.
Self-paced reading sets `lexsync_region_rts` and a question `question_response` and
`question_rt`. Each trial starts by clearing these, and before the logger a script
copies the trial's `condition`, `block` and `answer` from the text table into
`lexsync_condition`, `lexsync_block` and `lexsync_answer`. Both versions' loggers
write a variable without evaluating it. Before the loop, an inline script,
`lexsync_instructions`, shows the instructions and waits for the space bar, and
escape there stops the session. OpenSesame's canvas reads a subset of HTML, so the
script writes the text with `&`, `<` and `>` escaped and each line break as
`<br />`.

jsPsych is the browser target. A browser cannot address a parallel port, so the
trigger codes go into each trial's data and no marker leaves the machine. That
makes it suitable for behavioural work, for piloting and for sharing a procedure,
though never for EEG. The generated HTML embeds the events and the trials, opens
with a welcome screen that shows the instructions and waits for the space bar, and
saves responses locally, so no server is needed. The jsPsych library, its
keyboard-response plugin and its stylesheet load from a CDN, so the first run needs
an internet connection. Each of the three files
is loaded with Subresource Integrity, its SHA-384 and `crossorigin="anonymous"`, so
the browser refuses a copy that differs from the published release. A page that
collects participants' responses therefore runs only the code it was written with.
To run offline, point the tags at downloaded copies and serve the folder over http,
or remove each tag's `integrity` and `crossorigin` attributes. A browser refuses the
CORS request that a page opened from a `file://` address would make for a local
copy, so it could not check the hash. The word and its
response window are one jsPsych trial, recorded with `lexsync_event` set to
`target`. It accepts the response keys from the word's onset, shows the word for
its duration and runs on for the timeout. The first key ends it, so its `rt` is
timed from the word's onset.

Two smaller differences are worth knowing. The OpenSesame loop is written as
`sequential` on purpose, because its default is random, which would discard the
seeded trial order and make the three targets present different sequences. The
order is worth protecting, since it is computed from the design by a keyed-hash
shuffle and is identical in the R and Python engines. And the jsPsych exporter
maps the event model's key names onto browser key names, so `left` becomes
`arrowleft`, since the same event list has to mean the same thing to a browser as
to PsychoPy. It maps each trial's `answer` the same way, because jsPsych records the
key pressed by its browser name.

```{r loop-table}
psychopy_csv <- file.path(out, "vignette_experiment_english_psychopy.csv")
names(read.csv(psychopy_csv))
```

The trial table carries exactly the columns the events reference plus the
bookkeeping ones. A field no event mentions is not exported, which keeps the
generated table minimal and means the trial table is itself a readable statement
of what the experiment uses.

## Running a counterbalanced experiment

A design with more than one list, or with resampled item sets, has several
presentation versions. A version is one (replicate, list) pair of the presented
trials, and the versions are numbered from 1 in that order, so in a design without
replicates version *k* is list *k*. Each participant is presented one version.
Presenting them all would show each target of a Latin square in every condition,
which is the repetition the rotation exists to prevent, and every item sample of a
resampled design. Participant *p* runs version `((p - 1) mod V) + 1` of the *V*
versions, the rule `participant_table()` allocates by.

```{r versions}
two <- utils::modifyList(design, list(name = "vignette_two_lists",
                                      counterbalance = list(lists = 2)))
two_files <- export_experiments(counterbalance(stim, two, schema), two, schema, out)
basename(grep("\\.osexp$", two_files$files, value = TRUE))
participant_table(list(list = 1:2), 4)
```

The PsychoPy script runs the participant's version when launched as
`python <base>_psychopy.py --participant 3`. `--version 2` runs a version outright,
and so does `--list 2` in a design without replicates. Launched with none of these,
the script asks for the participant number and the version in a dialogue, where a
blank version takes the participant's by the rule. A version the script does not
have stops the run, with a message, before any window opens.

The jsPsych page reads the same choice from its address: `page.html?participant=3`,
`?version=2`, or `?list=2` without replicates, each a whole number from 1. A page
with more than one version, opened with none of these, shows a screen saying how to
open it and runs nothing. A static page cannot count its participants, so a study
recruited online without participant numbers hands out one `?version=k` link per
version. The welcome screen counts the trials of the version, every data row
carries the participant, the version, the list and the replicate, and the data file
is named `<title>_p<participant>_v<version>.csv`.

The OpenSesame target writes one experiment per version, as above:
`<base>_list<k>.osexp`, or `<base>_rep<r>_list<k>.osexp` when the versions span
several replicates. Each has its own loop and text tables, holding only that
version's trials, and the experimenter opens the participant's. At start-up, each
experiment compares the subject number OpenSesame asks for with its own version.
When that participant would normally run another one, it says so and waits for a
key. Space goes on with this file, and escape stops the session. A design with one
version and one trial order keeps `<base>.osexp`. The check runs once, before the
loop, so the experiment needs no run-if condition, a syntax that differs between
OpenSesame 3.3 and 4.x.

The datasheet records the number of versions as `counterbalancing$versions` and
the rule as `counterbalancing$assignment`, and its Methods text says that each
participant was presented one version. Its artefact list and the run log name every
file `export_experiments()` wrote, the loop and text tables included, since those
hold the trial order and the trigger codes the experiments present. The loop tables
keep each version's trials together, ordered by replicate, list and trial. They
carry `replicate` when the design has one. Item codes are allocated by set, so in a
resampled design an item code identifies an item only within its replicate, which
the `replicate` column tells apart.

With `counterbalance.orders: m` (see "Trial orders and runs of one condition"
above), each version also has m trial orders. Participant *p* runs order
`(((p - 1) div V) mod m) + 1`. In a two-list design with two orders, participants 1
and 2 run lists 1 and 2 in order 1, participants 3 and 4 run them in order 2, and
participant 5 starts the cycle again. The PsychoPy script and the jsPsych page sort
the version's trials by the participant's order, and a run without a participant
number presents order 1. Their data rows then carry the order, and their `trial`
column numbers the trials as presented. The OpenSesame target writes one experiment
per version and order, `<base>_list<k>_order<j>.osexp`
(`<base>_rep<r>_list<k>_order<j>.osexp` when the versions span several replicates,
and `<base>_order<j>.osexp` for a design with one version), whose check compares the
order as well as the version, and every trial logs `lexsync_order`.

## Trigger timing and the flip lock

This is the part that justifies generating the experiment at all. An ERP is
averaged over epochs cut around a marker, so the marker's timing error propagates
straight into the waveform. If the trigger is sent when the code decides to draw
the stimulus rather than when the display actually shows it, the error is the
interval between those two moments, which is up to one refresh (about 17 ms at
60 Hz) plus whatever the drawing code took, and it is variable from trial to
trial. A constant offset can be subtracted afterwards. Jitter cannot: it smears
the average and shrinks the component you are measuring.

The generated PsychoPy script never sends a trigger from the drawing sequence.
It registers the write with the window, to be executed on the next flip:

```
win.callOnFlip(port.setData, trigger)
```

`callOnFlip` defers the call until the flip that puts the stimulus on screen, so
the port write happens in the same operation that makes the stimulus visible.
That is the guarantee, and it is a property of the generated code. The Python
package's test suite pins it, driving the generated script against a mock PsychoPy
window and a mock port and asserting that the trigger is bound to the flip.

The reset is handled the same way. A recorder needs the line to return to zero
before the next code, so the script counts the hold down flip by flip and queues a
write of 0 on the flip that ends it. A code whose stimulus is shorter than the hold,
such as a one-flip prime, stays on the port through the events that follow and is
reset on that flip all the same. Only the next onset's code ends it sooner, with a 0
written just before the new code. The session markers, 254 before the first trial
and 255 after the last, are held the same way.

```{r trigger-settings}
str(schema$triggers)
```

`trigger_hold_ms` is 50, comfortably above the 10 ms minimum most recorders need
to register a pulse. The script converts it to the nearest whole number of flips at
the refresh it measures, and never to fewer than the flips that cover 10 ms. The
pulse therefore stays about 50 ms whether the display runs at 60 Hz or at 240 Hz,
where a hold of three frames, 50 ms at 60 Hz, would last 12.5 ms.
`reset_after_frames: N`, read only when `trigger_hold_ms` is not set, gives a hold
of N + 1 frames at `presentation.assumed_refresh_hz`. `inter_trigger_ms` is accepted
but not used, since the self-paced reading critical-region code is held like every
other code, and the run log says so when a schema sets it. `parallel_address` is
the LPT1 base address on a typical laboratory machine, and it is a schema value
because it belongs to the machine, which will run many designs.
`allow_code_overlap` is false, so a design whose item codes cannot all be kept
apart from its other codes is refused, as described under triggers above.

`backend` names the device both laboratory targets write the codes to. `parallel`,
the default, is the port at `parallel_address`. `serial` writes each code as one
byte to the device that `serial_port` names, at `baudrate` bits per second, 115200
unless set. A schema for a serial device therefore adds `backend: serial`, the port
as `serial_port: COM3` (`/dev/ttyUSB0` on Linux) and the rate the device's manual
gives. The port has to be named, and a serial backend without one is refused. A code
is held and reset on a serial device as on a parallel port, with a 0 written when its
hold is up. A serial line delays each code by an amount that varies from code to
code, and a parallel port does not. A USB-serial adapter carries each byte in a USB
transfer, scheduled in frames of a millisecond on a full-speed connection, and its
driver adds a delay of its own. Adapters built on FTDI chips also hold data on its
way to the computer until their latency timer runs out, 16 ms by default. That
matters for a device that answers and for a response box on the same adapter. The
photodiode checklist below measures the delay.

`mode` decides what happens when the device cannot be opened, as on a laptop with
no parallel port. Under `auto`, the default, both targets print each code in the
console, and a screen before any other tells the experimenter that no codes will be
sent. Pressing C goes on without them, and escape stops the run. Every trial records
the mode the run used, `hardware` or `mock`, as `trigger_mode` in the PsychoPy data
file and as `lexsync_trigger_mode` in the OpenSesame log. `hardware`
refuses to start without the device. The PsychoPy script stops before its window
opens, and the OpenSesame experiment stops in its setup. `mock` prints the codes
without trying the device, after the same notice.

OpenSesame reaches the same place by a different route, and the difference is
worth being explicit about. It has no `callOnFlip`, so the generated inline script
sends the trigger on the line after the canvas is shown:

```
_t0 = _lexsync_c_e1.show()
var.onset_time = _t0
_lexsync_onset(int(var.get(u'condition_trigger', _eval=False)), _t0)
```

This is sound because `show()` blocks until the display refresh and returns at it,
so the next statement runs immediately after the stimulus becomes visible. The
residual offset is the few microseconds of the return and the port write, and it
is constant rather than jittered. That makes it a close second to the flip lock,
which is why PsychoPy stays the reference target for EEG. The canvas was built in
the script's prepare phase, before the trial started, so nothing delays the show.
`_lexsync_onset` notes when the code is due to be reset, and the waits after it reset
the code once `trigger_hold_ms` has passed, in a later event when this one is
shorter. The setup script measures the frame period at start-up and logs it as
`lexsync_frame_ms`. Each event ends half a frame before its duration is up, so that
the next display lands on the refresh that ends it. OpenSesame's legacy clock
counts whole milliseconds, so the waits are kept to the millisecond, and so is a
hold that ends during one. A hold that ends while the experiment waits for the next
refresh lasts until that display, up to a frame longer. One that ends after the last
wait of a trial lasts until the next trial's first display. Between trials, the
logger and the next trial's prepare phase run while the last display stays up, so a
trial's last event lasts a little longer than its duration.

Neither generation nor its tests import PsychoPy, pyserial or any port driver.
Generation only writes text. The hardware is needed to *run* an experiment, not to
build one, which is what lets the whole demonstration reproduce on a laptop.

### Checking the timing

The durations above are what the generated code asks for, and what the Python
package's tests confirm on simulated displays. A real display adds delays no
software can see, such as an LCD's input lag. A study whose effect depends on a
duration or an onset should therefore be measured on the machine that will run it.
A photodiode on the screen, recorded by the same amplifier as the trigger port,
measures the display and the triggers on one clock.

1. Tape the photodiode over the place where the critical stimulus appears. White
   text on a black background drives most diodes. A small stimulus, such as a
   fixation cross, may need a white patch drawn with it for the pilot.
2. Run a pilot session on the laboratory machine, at the refresh rate and in the
   screen mode of the study, and record the diode and the trigger channel together.
   With `triggers.mode: hardware`, neither the pilot nor the study can start without
   the trigger device.
3. For each trial, measure the time from the trigger's onset to the diode's rise.
   It should be nearly constant. Its mean is the display's lag, which includes the
   time the screen takes to draw down to the diode and, on an LCD, an input lag
   that can exceed 10 ms. The analysis can subtract it. Its spread is the jitter an
   ERP average will carry.
4. Measure each critical stimulus from the diode's rise to its fall and compare it
   with the flips its duration asks for at that refresh rate: a 50 ms prime is
   three flips at 60 Hz and seven, 48.6 ms, at 144 Hz.
5. Measure the trigger pulses. Each should last about `trigger_hold_ms`, 50 ms by
   default, unless the next onset ends it sooner, and 254 should come before the
   first trial and 255 after the last.
6. Measure again after any change to the machine, the display, its refresh rate or
   the presentation software.

## Adding a paradigm

A design can override the event list outright, and this is the route that needs no
change to the package. The events below present a word twice with a mask between,
which no registered paradigm does, and both `text` events are triggered so the
recording can distinguish the two presentations.

```{r custom-events}
custom <- design
custom$name <- "vignette_custom"
custom$events <- list(
  list(type = "fixation", content = "+", duration_frames = 30L),
  list(type = "text", content = "{word}", duration_frames = 12L,
       trigger = 30L, onset_locked = TRUE),
  list(type = "mask", content = "#####", duration_frames = 6L),
  list(type = "text", content = "{word}", duration_frames = 48L,
       trigger = "condition", onset_locked = TRUE),
  list(type = "response", keys = c("left", "right"), timeout_ms = 2000L),
  list(type = "blank", duration_frames = 15L)
)
required_fields(custom)
custom_files <- export_experiments(stim, custom, schema, out)
basename(unlist(custom_files[c("psychopy", "opensesame", "jspsych")]))
```

Nothing in the backends changed. All three targets rendered a sequence they had
never seen, because each one walks the event list and knows nothing about
paradigms. Declaring events changes only the trial. The counterbalancing recipe
still follows the paradigm the design names, `factorial` here, so a priming
design that adjusts a duration keeps its Latin square, and a design that names no
paradigm counterbalances factorially.

To register a paradigm for reuse across designs, add an entry to the
`PARADIGMS` registry in `R/paradigms.R`, giving its `stimulus_fields`, its
`counterbalance` recipe and its `events`, and add the matching entry to
`python_workflow/src/lexsync/paradigms.py` so that the two engines stay in step.
Designs can then name it. The registry is a plain named list and the entries above
are the pattern to copy.

Adding a presentation target is the mirror image: write an `export_<target>()`
that walks the same rendered event list, and it will serve every paradigm at once.
